summary: This memo specifies an Encapsulating Security Payload based mechanism for sending user data packets with the Host Identity Protocol. It obsoletes RFC 5202.

plainLanguage.summary: HIP identifies hosts by public key rather than by address, and its handshake produces a shared secret. This RFC says how to use that secret to protect the data traffic that follows, by running the standard IPsec ESP format underneath HIP. The two hosts agree a cipher and swap the identifiers that will point to their shared keys, and the same handshake can later replace those keys.

questions: how does hip rekey an esp security association
what is beet mode in ipsec
subtitle: How two hosts that have authenticated with HIP turn their shared secret into ESP-protected data traffic.

tldr.problem: The Host Identity Protocol lets two hosts authenticate each other and agree a shared secret, but by itself it says nothing about how the data that follows should be carried or protected.
tldr.mechanism: The base exchange is extended with two new parameters, so that the hosts negotiate a cipher suite and swap the SPI values they will use, and the resulting keys are drawn from the same keying material the base exchange produced.
tldr.outcome: Each HIP association is linked to a pair of ESP security associations, one for each direction, and the UPDATE message from the base specification is extended so that those associations can be rekeyed later without tearing the HIP association down.

today:
RFC 7402 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 5202, so it is the current document for carrying user data over ESP with HIP.

The revision changed the set of cipher suites, deprecating several identifiers and making AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256 the mandatory implementation, and it replaced the older way of handling the SPI value. It also records that the HIP and ESP traffic has known middlebox traversal problems, and that other specifications exist for running HIP and ESP over UDP, with middlebox traversal itself out of scope.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In the Host Identity Protocol Architecture, hosts are identified with public keys, and the Host Identity Protocol base exchange allows any two HIP-supporting hosts to authenticate each other and create a HIP association between themselves. During the base exchange the hosts generate a piece of shared keying material using an authenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange.

The HIP base exchange specification does not describe any transport formats or methods for user data to be used during the actual communication. It only defines that it is mandatory to implement the Encapsulating Security Payload based transport format and method. This document specifies how ESP is used with HIP to carry actual user data: a set of HIP protocol extensions and their handling, using which a pair of ESP Security Associations is created between the hosts during the base exchange, with keys drawn from the keying material generated by that exchange. Once the HIP association and the required ESP security associations are established, the user data communication is protected using ESP, and the document also specifies methods to update an existing ESP security association.

Representations of Host Identity are not carried explicitly in the headers of user data packets. Instead, the ESP Security Parameter Index is used to indicate the right host context, and the SPIs are selected during the HIP ESP setup exchange. For user data packets the ESP SPIs, possibly in combination with IP addresses, are used indirectly to identify the host context, which avoids any additional explicit protocol headers.

HIP and ESP traffic have known issues with middlebox traversal, and other specifications exist for operating HIP and ESP over UDP. Middlebox traversal is out of scope for this document. The document obsoletes RFC 5202.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a HIP host is known by its public key rather than its address, the data packets do not need to carry that key around. A short number in the packet header is enough to point to the right keys, and the two hosts agree that number during the handshake.

sections.title: Using ESP with HIP
sections.content:
The HIP base exchange sets up a HIP association between two hosts. It provides two-way host authentication and key material generation, but no means for protecting the data communication that follows, and this document specifies the use of ESP for that purpose. The use of ESP described here is intended only for host-to-host traffic, and security gateways are not supported.

To support ESP, the HIP base exchange messages need minor additions. In the R1 packet the Responder adds the possible ESP transforms in an ESP_TRANSFORM parameter before sending it to the Initiator. The Initiator receives the proposed transforms, selects one, and adds it to the I2 packet in an ESP_TRANSFORM parameter. In the I2 packet the Initiator also sends the SPI value it wants to be used for ESP traffic flowing from the Responder to the Initiator, carried in the ESP_INFO parameter. When the ESP security association setup is finalised, the Responder sends its own SPI value to the Initiator in the R2 packet, again using ESP_INFO.

The ESP packet looks exactly the same as the IPsec ESP transport format packet, though the semantics differ in some respects. One way to implement packet processing is so that a standards compliant, unmodified IPsec implementation can be used with some additional transport checksum processing above it, with IP addresses used as indexes to the right host context. For outgoing packets the implementation recalculates the upper-layer checksums using Host Identity Tags, and then changes the packet source and destination addresses back to the corresponding IP addresses before handing the packet to IPsec ESP for transport mode handling. On reception the packet is first put through IPsec ESP transport mode handling, and after decryption the source and destination IP addresses are replaced with the Host Identity Tags, and the upper-layer checksums are verified before the packet is passed to the upper layer.

An alternative is the BEET mode, Bound End-to-End Tunnel, described in Appendix B. In BEET mode the ESP packet is formatted as a transport mode packet, but the semantics of the connection are the same as for tunnel mode: the outer addresses of the packet are the IP addresses and the inner addresses are the Host Identity Tags. BEET mode is entirely internal to a host and does not require the peer to implement it, since the peer can use ESP transport mode and do the address conversions outside ESP.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways to build the packets are described. The first keeps a normal IPsec implementation and adds a step that rewrites the addresses to the host identities and recalculates the checksums around them. The second, BEET mode, rewrites the IP header after the packet has been encrypted, so the addresses on the wire are ordinary IP addresses and the host identities stay inside the encrypted part.

sections.title: The ESP_INFO Parameter
sections.content:
During the establishment and update of an ESP security association, the SPI value of both hosts must be transmitted between them, and the hosts also need the index value into the keying material from which they draw keys. The ESP_INFO parameter carries the SPI values and the keying material index between the hosts. It has type 65 and length 12, and its fields are a Reserved field that is zero when sent, a KEYMAT Index, an OLD SPI and a NEW SPI.

The KEYMAT Index is the index, in bytes, where to continue drawing ESP keys from the keying material. If the packet includes a new Diffie-Hellman key and the ESP_INFO is sent in an UPDATE packet, the field must be zero; if the ESP_INFO is included in the base exchange messages, it must carry the index of the point from which the ESP security association keys are drawn. The length of the field limits how much keying material can be drawn, and if that amount is exceeded the packet must contain a new Diffie-Hellman key.

The OLD SPI is the old SPI for data sent to the addresses associated with this association, and is zero in an initial setup. The NEW SPI is the new SPI for data sent to those addresses. During the initial setup the hosts send the SPI value they want the peer to use when sending ESP data to them, set in the NEW SPI field, and the OLD SPI field is set to zero. It may also be zero when additional security associations are set up between HIP hosts, as in the multihomed case, although that use is beyond the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This parameter is how the two ends tell each other which numbers to put in the packet headers, and how far into the agreed keying material to start taking keys. The old number is blank the first time, because there is no earlier number to replace.

sections.title: The ESP_TRANSFORM Parameter
sections.content:
The ESP_TRANSFORM parameter is used during ESP security association establishment. The first party sends a selection of transform families in the parameter, and the peer must select one of the proposed values and include it in the response parameter. It has type 4095, and its length is measured in octets excluding the type, the length and the padding; the Reserved field is zero when sent and ignored when received; and each Suite ID defines the ESP suite to be used.

The suite identifiers are assigned as follows. Zero is reserved, 1 is AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA1, 2 to 6 are deprecated, 7 is NULL with HMAC-SHA-256, 8 is AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256, 9 is AES-256-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256, 10 is AES-CCM-8, 11 is AES-CCM-16, 12 is AES-GCM with an 8-octet ICV, 13 is AES-GCM with a 16-octet ICV, 14 is AES-CMAC-96, and 15 is AES-GMAC.

The sender of an ESP transform parameter must make sure there are no more than six Suite IDs in one parameter, and a recipient must be prepared to handle received parameters that contain more than six. The limited number of suite identifiers sets the maximum size of the parameter. As the default configuration the parameter must contain at least one of the mandatory suite identifiers, though a configuration option may allow the administrator to override this default. The mandatory implementation is AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256, and NULL with HMAC-SHA-256 should also be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The transform parameter is a menu of cipher suites. One side lists what it is willing to use, and the other picks one. The list is capped at six entries so the parameter stays a predictable size, and every implementation has to offer AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256.

sections.title: Setting Up and Updating an ESP Association
sections.content:
Setting up an ESP security association between hosts using HIP is done by including parameters in the last three messages of the four-message HIP base exchange. The R1 message carries the ESP_TRANSFORM parameter, in which the sending host defines the possible ESP transforms it is willing to use; including it adds clarity to the transport format list, although it may initiate negotiations for possibly unselected transforms, and resource-constrained devices will most likely restrict support to a single transform to keep the ROM overhead down. The I2 message contains the response: the sender must select one of the transforms proposed in R1 and include it, and it also includes the ESP_INFO parameter with the SPI value to be used by the peer host. The R2 message finalises the setup and contains the SPI information the Initiator needs.

Each HIP association is linked to two ESP security associations, one for incoming packets and one for outgoing packets. The Initiator's incoming association corresponds with the Responder's outgoing one, and vice versa. The Initiator defines the SPI for its incoming association, and the Responder creates its outgoing association as part of processing the I2 message, before sending the R2. The initial session keys are drawn from the generated keying material after the HIP keys have been drawn, and when the HIP association is removed the related ESP security associations must be removed as well.

An existing association may need updating during the lifetime of the HIP association, for example because of sequence number rollover. The update is done with three messages using the UPDATE mechanism from the HIP base specification. The host willing to update creates and sends an UPDATE message carrying an ESP_INFO parameter with the old SPI value, the new SPI value and the index into the keying material from which the next keys will be drawn; if new keying material must be generated, the message also carries a Diffie-Hellman parameter. The host receiving it must reply with an UPDATE message carrying the corresponding values, and with a Diffie-Hellman parameter if the incoming message had one.

Because the base exchange has finished by the time a rekey happens, there are no longer Initiator and Responder roles and the association is symmetric; the party that starts the rekey is denoted I' and its peer R'. The peer does not take the new outgoing association into use at once, so two pairs of associations temporarily exist towards the same peer. The party that started the rekey starts using the new outgoing association immediately, and the peer starts using its new outgoing association when it receives traffic on the new incoming association or the acknowledgement confirming that the rekey is complete, after which the old associations can be removed.

Two NOTIFICATION error types are defined for describing errors in the ESP transform negotiation: NO_ESP_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN, value 18, meaning that none of the proposed crypto suites was acceptable, and INVALID_ESP_TRANSFORM_CHOSEN, value 19, meaning that the chosen suite does not correspond to one offered by the Responder.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup rides on the existing handshake, so no extra round trip is needed. The rekey later uses a three-message exchange, and both sides keep the old keys working until the new ones are confirmed, so no packets are lost while the change happens.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
The keying material is generated as described in the HIP base specification, and during the base exchange the initial keys are drawn from the generated material. After the HIP association keys have been drawn, the ESP keys are drawn in a fixed order: the ESP encryption key for the outgoing traffic of the host with the greater Host Identity Tag, the ESP authentication key for the outgoing traffic of that same host, then the ESP encryption key for the outgoing traffic of the host with the lower tag, and finally that host's ESP authentication key. HOST_g denotes the host with the greater HIT value and HOST_l the host with the lower one, and when HIT values are compared they are interpreted as positive, unsigned 128-bit integers in network byte order.

The four HIP keys are only drawn from the keying material during a base exchange. Subsequent rekeys using UPDATE draw only the four ESP keys from it.

The number of bits drawn for a given algorithm is the natural size of the keys, as specified in the HIP base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Both hosts come out of the handshake with the same long string of random bytes, and they each take the next four chunks from it in a fixed order, so that both end up with the same four keys without sending them. The order is fixed by comparing the two host identities, so both sides compute the same order without any extra negotiation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for ESP are discussed in the ESP specification. There are different ways to establish an ESP security association between two nodes, for example using IKE, and this document specifies how the Host Identity Protocol is used instead. The issues that are new or changed from standard ESP usage are the initial keying material generation and the updating of the keying material.

The initial keying material is generated using the Host Identity Protocol and the Diffie-Hellman procedure. The document extends the use of the UPDATE packet, defined in the base specification, to modify existing ESP security associations, and the hosts may rekey, forcing the generation of new keying material with the Diffie-Hellman procedure. The initial setup of the security associations is done during the base exchange, and that message exchange is protected using the methods provided by the base exchange. Changes in connection parameters basically mean that the old security association is removed and a new one generated once the UPDATE exchange has completed, and that exchange is protected using the HIP association keys. Both an HMAC and signing of packets are used.
sections.plainLanguage: The one thing that differs from ordinary IPsec is where the keys come from. Instead of a separate key exchange protocol, the keys come from the HIP handshake, and the same handshake's update message is reused to replace them later. The setup and the rekey exchanges are themselves protected by the HIP association.

messages.label: R1: ESP_TRANSFORM
messages.note: The Responder offers the ESP transforms it is willing to use.

messages.label: I2: ESP_TRANSFORM, ESP_INFO
messages.note: The Initiator picks one transform and sends the SPI it wants for traffic from the Responder.

messages.label: R2: ESP_INFO
messages.note: The Responder sends its own SPI and the keying material index.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent, ignored when received.

fields.name: KEYMAT Index
fields.desc: The index, in bytes, where to continue drawing ESP keys from the keying material.

fields.name: OLD SPI
fields.desc: The old SPI for data sent to the addresses associated with this association; zero in an initial setup.

fields.name: NEW SPI
fields.desc: The new SPI for data sent to the addresses associated with this association.

items.label: AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA1
items.desc: The older suite carried over from RFC 5202.

items.label: NULL with HMAC-SHA-256
items.desc: Authentication only, no encryption. Should also be supported.

items.label: AES-256-CBC with HMAC-SHA-256
items.desc: A longer key with the same mode.

items.label: AES-GCM, 8-octet ICV
items.desc: Galois counter mode with a short tag.

items.label: AES-GCM, 16-octet ICV
items.desc: Galois counter mode with a long tag.

items.label: AES-GMAC
items.desc: Galois counter mode with a GMAC tag.

messages.label: UPDATE(ESP_INFO, SEQ, DIFFIE_HELLMAN)
messages.note: Carries the old SPI, the new SPI and the keying material index.

messages.label: UPDATE(ESP_INFO, SEQ, ACK, DIFFIE_HELLMAN)
messages.note: The peer answers with the corresponding values.
